2x or 4x oversampling of the nonlinear stages (polyphase IIR half-band filters, no latency).
Final output level.
Noise gate keyed from the input: below the threshold the amp's output fades out (6 dB hysteresis, 30 ms hold); -90 dB turns it off.

arpeggiator.properties: A MIDI effect: MIDI in, MIDI out, the audio passes through untouched (place it before an instrument). Steps fall on a grid locked to the host's beat position while it plays (a held chord starts on the next step); while it is stopped the arpeggio runs at the tempo from the first key. The sequence is the held notes by pitch (or as played) over the octaves; each step plays one note, or every note for Chord, for Gate % of the step, with the played velocity times the step's lane value. Every note sent is ended: releasing the last key (without Latch), all notes off (CC 120/123) and the transport stopping end the arpeggio's notes at once; a pitch played twice in a row starts again cleanly. Controllers, pitch bend and other messages pass through. The Random pattern uses an exact Park-Miller sequence from Seed. Sample-accurate and the same in the JSFX, the GFX version and the VST3/CLAP.

uses: A first compressor on a vocal without knowing the settings

assisted_comp.properties: Learn: level histogram of 50 ms windows (0.1 dB bins, only windows above -60 dBFS count), mean crest factor, onset intervals (a 5 ms envelope jumping 6 dB over a 100 ms one) and BS.1770 integrated loudness. Rules (tools/assisted_targets.json): the target's reduction on the loud parts times Amount sets the threshold; ratio per source plus a target step (1.5:1-10:1); attack 5-25 ms by crest factor times the target's factor; release 60% of the onset interval (50-500 ms); makeup gives back half the reduction; Podcast moves Output to -16 LUFS. Compressor: stereo-linked peak detector → 6 dB soft knee → attack/release smoothing → makeup → Mix → Output. No AI: fixed rules, the same result every time. Zero latency.

How long the filter envelope takes to fall back (5 ms to 3 s): short for plucks and acid, long for slow sweeps.
The amplitude envelope's attack time (1 ms to 2 s).
The time to fall from the peak to the Sustain level (5 ms to 5 s).
The level held while the key is down (0 to 100%); at 0 every note decays away like an 808.
The time the note takes to fade after the key is released (5 ms to 5 s).
Legato: a key pressed while another is held glides to its pitch without a new attack; Always: every note glides from the last pitch and starts again.
The glide time (0 to 1000 ms); 0 jumps straight to the new pitch. Phrase slides use at least 60 ms.
How much the velocity changes the level and the filter envelope (0% = every note the same).

The phrase the bass plays while a key from C2 up is held, in 16ths at the host's tempo (Eighths, Octaves, Offbeat, Gallop, Funk, Acid, Tresillo, Trap); the keys C1 (Off) to G#1 choose it too. Off plays the keys as they are.
The output level (-24 to +12 dB).
uses: Sub and 808 bass lines for trap, hip-hop and pop, with glides between notes
Squelchy acid lines with resonance, accents and slides
Wide detuned Reese basses for drum and bass and dubstep
Instant grooves: hold one key and the phrase player plays a bass line in time with the song
Switch phrases live with the keys below C2 while the right hand sets the root
bass.properties: An instrument: MIDI in, stereo out (the same signal on both sides), no samples. One monophonic voice with last-note priority: releasing a key goes back to a key still held. Saw and Square are band-limited (PolyBLEP); the low-pass is two state-variable stages (24 dB per octave), the second one resonant, with an exponential envelope; Drive is a soft clipper after the filter; the amplitude has an ADSR with linear attack and exponential decay and release, so notes start and stop without clicks. Pitch bend covers +-2 semitones. The phrase player follows the host's beat while it plays (from the first key while it is stopped), assumes 4/4 and restarts the bar every 16 steps; the keys from C1 to G#1 (MIDI notes 24 to 32) choose the phrase, the newest key held from C2 (36) up sets its root, and a new root while a note sounds retunes it. All notes off (CC 123/120) releases everything. Sample-accurate and the same in the JSFX, the GFX version and the VST3/CLAP.

Moves the lowest notes of the chord up an octave: root position, first, second or third inversion.

chords.properties: A MIDI effect: MIDI in, MIDI out, the audio passes through untouched (place it before an instrument). Chords are stacked in thirds inside the scale (sus2/sus4 swap the third for the second or fourth), then inverted, voiced, moved by octaves and kept within 0 to 127. Every note-on sent is remembered with the key that made it, so the key's release always ends exactly those notes, whatever was changed meanwhile; strum notes still waiting are dropped; a note two keys share sounds until both are released; all notes off (CC 120/123) releases every key of its channel. Pitch bend, controllers and sustain pass through; poly pressure goes to every note of the key's chord. Sample-accurate and the same in the JSFX, the GFX version and the VST3/CLAP.

draw_eq.keywords: draw eq drawable equalizer curve graphic eq 10 band ten band octave smooth tone shaping tilt smile air low end mud telephone spectrum analyzer mix
slider_desc: Gain at 31 Hz (-18 to +18 dB): the sub and deep low end; drag the first point in the curve.
Gain at 63 Hz (-18 to +18 dB): kick and bass weight.
Gain at 125 Hz (-18 to +18 dB): bass body and warmth.
Gain at 250 Hz (-18 to +18 dB): low mids, where mud and boxiness build up.
Gain at 500 Hz (-18 to +18 dB): body of voices, guitars and snares.
Gain at 1 kHz (-18 to +18 dB): the centre of the midrange, nasal or honky when boosted.
Gain at 2 kHz (-18 to +18 dB): presence and attack.
Gain at 4 kHz (-18 to +18 dB): clarity and edge, harsh if pushed.
Gain at 8 kHz (-18 to +18 dB): brilliance and sibilance.
Gain at 16 kHz (-18 to +18 dB): air and sparkle (left out at sample rates below 36 kHz).
How smoothly the curve flows between the points (0 to 100%): low values give each point its own defined bump, high values blend them into broad, gentle slopes.
Level after the EQ (-18 to +18 dB), to match loudness after big boosts or cuts.
Blend of equalized and dry signal (0 to 100%), for subtle or parallel tone shaping.
uses: Sketch a tone curve by dragging across the display instead of setting bands one by one
Gentle tilts and smiles on a mix bus or master
Carve mud and add air on vocals, guitars and pads
Telephone and old radio voices with steep cuts at both ends
Match a reference by drawing against the live spectrum behind the curve
draw_eq.properties: Ten points at fixed octave-spaced frequencies (31.25 Hz to 16 kHz) set the gain the curve passes through. Each point drives an RBJ peaking filter; the ten gains are solved (Gaussian elimination on the filters' interaction, then two corrections with the true response) so the cascade passes through every point to within a fraction of a dB, and Smoothness sets the filters' Q from 1.5 to 0.6. Minimum-phase IIR, zero latency; with every point at 0 dB the filters are bypassed and the plugin is transparent. Mix with the dry signal, then Output. The GFX and VST3/CLAP interfaces draw the response over a live output spectrum: drag across the display to draw, double-click a point to reset it.

drum_machine.properties: An instrument: MIDI in, stereo out (or four stereo pairs with Outputs Groups), no samples. Ten synthesized voices after the classic drum machines: a sine kick with click and pitch sweep, a two-tone snare with noise, a three-burst clap, rim/clave, closed and open hats and a cymbal from six detuned squares (the closed hat chokes the open one), two toms with pitch sweep and a two-square cowbell. A 16-step sequencer locked to the host's beat while it plays: steps are hit, accent, flam, roll or chance (half the time), each track has its own length (1 to 16 steps), with swing up to 75%. Probability and Generate draw from an exact Park-Miller sequence from Seed, so a pattern always comes back the same. General MIDI drum notes (36 kick, 38 snare, 39 clap, 37 rim, 42 closed hat, 46 open hat, toms, 56 cowbell, 49 cymbal) play the voices at any time, with velocity. Drive is a soft clipper and Grit a sample-and-hold with bit reduction on the whole kit. Sample-accurate and the same in the JSFX, the GFX version and the VST3/CLAP. Song mode chains up to 8 sections (a pattern for 1 to 16 bars each), counted from the start of the project.

humanize.properties: A MIDI effect: MIDI in, MIDI out, the audio passes through untouched (place it before an instrument). A MIDI effect cannot send a note before it arrives, so everything goes out a fixed latency later (Timing plus Push's move), reported for delay compensation; each note-on then moves by a random amount within ±Timing plus the groove's shift at its place in the beat (the host's beat while it plays, a beat at the tempo while it is stopped). A note-off follows the groove at its own place and never comes before its note-on; a pitch two notes share starts again cleanly; all notes off releases the channel's notes first; other messages keep their place, the latency later. The random numbers are an exact Park-Miller sequence from Seed, started again at every transport start. Sample-accurate and the same in the JSFX, the GFX version and the VST3/CLAP.

organ.properties: An instrument: MIDI in, stereo out, no samples, 16 voices (a 17th key takes the oldest voice, released ones first, after a 1.5 ms fade). Each key sums its nine drawbars as sines at the harmonics 1/2, 3/2, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 of its pitch, made from one sine and cosine per key; like tonewheels the harmonics fold back an octave above 5.9 kHz and below 32 Hz. Keys start and stop with 1.5 and 6 ms ramps; velocity does nothing, as on the original. The sum passes the vibrato scanner (a delay swept at 6.9 Hz), the preamp (a soft clipper) and the rotary speaker of NULL Rotary Speaker (an 800 Hz crossover, horn and drum with Doppler and tremolo, two microphones). CC 11 is expression (smoothed), the mod wheel (CC 1) at 64 and up switches the rotor speed, all notes off (CC 123/120) releases every key. Sample-accurate and the same in the JSFX, the GFX version and the VST3/CLAP.

slider_desc: What is aligned to what: Right to Left moves the right channel against the left, Track to Sidechain moves the track against a reference on channels 3/4 (reports a fixed 10 ms latency so it can also move the track earlier).

Flips the polarity of the left channel (of the track's left channel in Sidechain mode).
Flips the polarity of the right channel (of the track's right channel in Sidechain mode).
Turns the phase of the moved signal by this angle at the Focus frequency (0 to 360 degrees; 0 and 360 = off), for low end that a time shift alone cannot line up.
The frequency where Rotation is exact (20 to 1000 Hz): set it to the fundamental that matters, such as the kick or bass note.
Mono Sum plays the moved signal added to its reference, so you can hear when the two are fullest together; Normal plays the result.
uses: Line up kick in and kick out, or snare top and bottom mics
Align a bass DI with its amp or cabinet mic
Check and fix polarity on multi-mic recordings
Undo a Haas delay or fix a stereo pair recorded with a timing offset

phase_align.properties: Delay line per channel with whole-sample exact reads and 4-point Catmull-Rom interpolation for fractions; per-channel polarity; Rotation by two first-order all-pass filters, each turning half the angle at Focus (less below it, more above). Right to Left needs no latency: a negative delay delays the left channel instead. Track to Sidechain delays the track by ceil(10 ms) + 1 samples less the delay and reports that as latency, so the track can also move ahead of the reference; the reference is only listened to (Mono Sum) and metered. The GFX and VST3/CLAP interfaces show the phase difference across frequency, the total delay, the latency and the correlation of the two signals (full band and below 150 Hz). In REAPER, send the reference to channels 3/4 of the track.

slider_desc: The string instrument: Nylon Guitar, Steel Guitar, Harp, Koto, Pipa, Banjo, Muted Guitar or Dulcimer, each with its own decay, brightness, attack and body.
Where the string is plucked, as a share of its length (5 to 50%): near the bridge it is thin and bright, at the middle round and hollow.
How bright the pluck and the string are (0 to 100%), from a soft thumb to a hard pick.
Scales how long the strings ring (10 to 300%); low strings ring longer than high ones.
How fast a string is damped when its key comes up (10 ms to 2 s); the sustain pedal holds the strings until it is lifted.
How much of the instrument's body resonance is heard (0 to 100%).
Spreads the strings across the stereo field by pitch and widens the body (0 to 100%).
How much the key velocity changes the level and the brightness of the pluck (0% plays every note the same).
Off plays every key as you press it; Down, Up, Down-Up, Folk and Offbeat strum the chord you hold in time with the host's tempo (on its beat while it plays, from the first key while it is stopped).
How often the chord is strummed: quarters, eighths, sixteenths or eighth-note triplets.
The time from one string to the next within a strum (0 to 100 ms): short for a tight chop, long for a slow roll.
The output level (-24 to +12 dB).
Pizzicato: plays plucked violins or cellos instead of the Model: a finger's soft pluck, a short decay and the instrument's wooden body; Off uses the Model.
MPE: On for an MPE controller: on channels 2-16 each note gets its own pitch bend (the string's length, down to 30 Hz) and pressure (louder, up to +6 dB); Off treats every channel alike.
MPE Bend Range: how far a note's own pitch bend goes (48 semitones is the MPE default).
uses: Strummed acoustic rhythm guitar from held chords, synced to the song
Fingerpicked nylon guitar and harp lines and arpeggios
Koto and pipa melodies with the twang of the string
Reggae skanks and funk sixteenths with muted, short strums
Banjo rolls, dulcimer and plucked textures for folk and film
pluck.properties: An instrument: MIDI in, stereo out, no samples, 12 voices (a note played again lets go of the string still sounding in 40 ms and takes a new voice; a 13th takes the oldest voice, released ones first, after a 2 ms fade). Each note is a Karplus-Strong string: a delay line one period long, read with interpolation and corrected for the loop filter so it is in tune, a one-pole low-pass and a loop gain from the decay time at the pitch. The pluck is low-passed noise and the triangle of a string pulled at Pick Position, combed at that position; Koto, Pipa and Banjo start slightly sharp and settle. The strings pass the model's body (three resonances) and a DC blocker. The strummer plays the keys held (or held by the sustain pedal, CC 64) at Strum Rate on the host's beat, low to high (down) or high to low (up), Strum Spread apart; up strums in Down-Up and Folk hit the top four strings, the beat's strums are louder. All notes off (CC 123/120) stops everything. Sample-accurate and the same in the JSFX, the GFX version and the VST3/CLAP.

reference.keywords: reference track a/b compare comparison level match loudness matched lufs short-term mix mastering correlation spectrum mono check side
slider_desc: What you hear: the Track (your mix, channels 1/2) or the Reference (channels 3/4); the switch crossfades over 10 ms.
Level Match: plays the reference at your mix's short-term loudness, so the comparison is about tone and balance, not volume.
Extra gain on the reference (-12 to +12 dB), on top of the match.
Monitor: Stereo, Mono (both channels summed) or Side (the difference only), for both sources.
uses: A/B a mix against a commercial track at the same loudness
Check a master's tonal balance and width against a reference

reference.properties: Both inputs are K-weighted (ITU-R BS.1770) and measured as short-term loudness (the last 3 s, every 100 ms). With Level Match on, the reference's gain moves a tenth of the way to the difference every 100 ms (about a second to settle), within ±24 dB, and holds while either source is below -60 LUFS; Trim is added. Listen crossfades linearly over 10 ms. Monitor folds after the switch. The interfaces show both loudnesses, the reference's gain, each source's stereo correlation (averaged over about 3 s) and both spectra (each bin averaged over about a second, the reference at its played gain). No latency, no Rack module (it needs a second stereo input).

resonance_suppressor.keywords: resonance suppressor soothe detroubler dynamic eq spectral harshness resonances tame fft mixing mastering vocals guitars de-harsh
slider_desc: Maximum reduction per frequency.
How narrow the peaks it targets are: the spectral envelope is averaged over 2 octaves at 0% down to 1/8 octave at 100%.
How far a frequency must rise above the envelope before it is reduced (2 to 12 dB).
How fast the reduction grabs, per FFT frame.
How fast the reduction lets go.
Lowest frequency processed (fades out over half an octave below).
Highest frequency processed (fades out over half an octave above).
Soft: 2:1 with a 6 dB knee, easing into Depth. Hard: removes all of the excess, up to Depth.

uses: Taming harsh resonances in vocals, guitars and cymbals
Smoothing ringing room modes and boxy recordings
Gentle de-harshing on buses and masters
Finding problem frequencies with Delta
resonance_suppressor.properties: STFT with 2048-point FFT, 75% overlap and sqrt-Hann windows; both channels in one complex FFT, linked detection on their mean power. Each bin's level is compared with a log-frequency moving average of the spectrum; the excess over the Selectivity threshold sets the reduction (Soft or Hard), smoothed per frame (Attack/Release) and across neighbouring bins, limited to Low–High Freq. Perfect reconstruction when nothing is reduced. Latency: 2047 samples (reported to the host).

resonator.properties: Signal chain: Input → 20 Hz High-Pass → up to 4 Karplus-Strong string loops per channel (one per chord note) → DC Blocker → Soft Ceiling → Mix → Output. Each loop is a delay line, a first-order allpass for the fractional part of the period and a linear-phase 3-tap low-pass, so every harmonic is exactly in tune. The loop gain sets the decay of the fundamental and stays below 1, the input to each loop is scaled for unity noise power, and the wet sum has a soft ceiling at 0 dBFS, so it can ring but never run away. No latency.

slider_desc: Scales all delay lengths (25–100% of full size); larger values give longer, sparser reflections and a longer tail.
Comb feedback; higher values give a longer tail (roughly 0.4 s to 4 s at default size).
High-frequency absorption in the tail: 0% is bright, higher values make the tail progressively darker (low-pass from 16 kHz down to 1.2 kHz).
Blend between dry signal and reverb.
Passes the input unprocessed when set to 1.
Delays the signal feeding the reverb (0–250 ms) so the tail starts after the dry sound; the dry signal is not delayed.
12 dB/oct high-pass on the reverb only, to keep the tail out of the low end; off at 20 Hz.
12 dB/oct low-pass on the reverb only, for a darker, less splashy tail; off at 20 kHz.
Stereo width of the reverb (mid/side): 0% is mono, 100% unchanged, 200% extra wide.
Slow, gentle movement of the internal delay lengths that smears metallic ringing and gives the tail a chorused shimmer; 0% is off.
Holds the current tail forever: the loop stops losing level and no new input enters, for pads and drones.
Classic is the original room algorithm; Plate adds dense input diffusion and a brighter tail; Hall adds the diffusion with longer, wider delays for a bigger, smoother space.
Dips the reverb while the dry signal is loud, so the tail fills the gaps between phrases and hits
Gated reverb: above -80 dB the tail stays open while the input is above this level, then is cut (-80 = off)
How long the gate stays open after the input falls under the threshold
uses: Room and hall ambience on dry sources

reverb.properties: Input → mono sum → four damped feedback combs per side (right side slightly longer for a decorrelated stereo tail) → two series all-passes per side → Dry/Wet Mix → Output. Delay lengths and damping are scaled to the sample rate, so it sounds the same at 44.1, 48 or 96 kHz; zero latency.

riff.keywords: midi riff generator melody generator pattern step sequencer random seed tempo sync arpeggio bassline lead hook key scale pentatonic blues rhythm lock accent
slider_desc: The key the riff is in.
The scale the riff's notes come from (major, minor, harmonic or melodic minor, the modes, major or minor pentatonic, blues); the key you hold starts the riff on the scale note at or below it.
Picks the riff (1 to 999): every seed is a different pattern, and the same seed always plays the same riff, in REAPER and in every DAW.
How many of the steps play a note (0 to 100%); the first step always plays, the others are rests when they miss.
The length of the pattern in steps (4 to 32) before it repeats; more steps add to the end of the same riff.
The step length, synced to the tempo: 1/8, 1/16 or 1/32 notes, or their triplets.
How far the riff climbs above the key you hold: 1 to 3 octaves of the scale.
How long each note lasts as a share of its step (10 to 100%): short values play staccato, 100% plays legato.
Keeps a rhythm while Seed rolls new notes: 0 is Off (the rhythm follows Seed); any other value plays the rhythm of that seed (the LOCK RHYTHM switch in the display sets it to the current seed).
How much the step velocities vary below the velocity of the key you hold (0% plays every step at it).
The share of steps that are accented, played well above the others (0 to 100%).
How often a step plays a new note instead of repeating the note one beat earlier (0% repeats a one-beat motif, 100% is all new notes).
uses: Hold one key and get basslines, leads or hooks that are always in key
Roll through seeds to find a riff, then lock its rhythm and change only the notes
Tempo-synced arpeggio-like runs and triplet rolls from a single held key
Transpose a riff live: the key you hold is its root, the last key pressed leads
Feed any synth or sampler with endless, repeatable melodic ideas
riff.properties: A MIDI effect: MIDI in, MIDI out, the audio passes through untouched (place it before an instrument). The pattern comes from two separate Park-Miller random streams seeded by Seed: one for the rhythm (which steps play, their velocity and accents), one for the pitches (root jumps, steps and skips, motif repeats), so it is fully deterministic and Rhythm Lock can keep one while the other changes. While the host plays, the steps sit on its beat grid (the step is the beat position divided by the rate, modulo Steps); stopped, the riff starts with the key and runs at the host's tempo. One note sounds at a time and every note-on gets its note-off; releasing every key, all notes off (CC 120/123) or the transport stopping ends the riff. Pitch bend, controllers and sustain pass through; poly pressure of the leading key goes to the note sounding. Sample-accurate and the same in the JSFX, the GFX version and the VST3/CLAP.

slicer.properties: Signal chain: Input → two bar buffers (4 beats at the host tempo, one recording while the other plays) → previous bar cut into 8/16/32 slices → slice order and per-slice reverse, repeat (first half twice) and backspin from Pattern, Variation and the chances, all drawn from a Park-Miller generator seeded by Seed → Gate shortens each slice → 2.5 ms fades at every cut (slices that continue the audio seamlessly are not faded) → Mix with the dry signal → Output. The output runs one bar behind (a musical delay, not reported as latency); until the first bar is recorded the input passes through. While the transport plays the bar is locked to the song position; stopped, it free-runs at the host tempo (40 to 300 bpm, 4/4).

slider_desc: The bed it pans into: 5.1, 7.1 or 7.1.4, on the pins L R C LFE Ls Rs Lrs Rrs Ltf Rtf Ltr Rtr (the pins a format does not use stay silent).
Mono pans one source and spreads it; Stereo places the left and right inputs either side of Azimuth.
Where the sound sits around the room, from -180 to 180 degrees, 0 in front, negative to the left.
How high the sound sits in 7.1.4, from 0 (ear level) to 90 degrees (overhead).
Mono: how wide the source is spread (0 to 180 degrees). Stereo: the angle between left and right (60 is the front pair).
How much of a front sound plays from the centre speaker; below 100 % it moves into a phantom centre between L and R.
Sends the mono sum through a 120 Hz low-pass to the LFE, from -60 dB (Off) to 0 dB.
Gain on every pin (-24 to +12 dB).
uses: Place a stereo music stem or a mono effect in a 5.1 or 7.1 mix
Put pads, ambiences and flyovers above the listener in 7.1.4

Feed the LFE from a bass or an effect
surround_panner.properties: Pairwise power-normalised VBAP on the ear-level ring (speakers as ITU-R BS.775 / BS.2051: L/R at 30 degrees, 5.1 surrounds at 110, 7.1 sides at 90 and rears at 150, tops at 45 and 135 degrees, elevation 45). Elevation crossfades the power from the ear level to the tops. A mono source with Spread is seven points with their powers averaged, so its level stays the same. The LFE send is a 4th-order Linkwitz-Riley low-pass at 120 Hz. The gains glide over about 20 ms. No latency. Twelve output pins: in REAPER set the track to 12 channels and route the pins to your bed. The player on this site plays pins 1 and 2 only.

slider_desc: Engine: Analog (two classic oscillators) or Wavetable (both oscillators read the selected table).
Osc 1's wave in the Analog engine: Saw, Square (both band-limited), Triangle or Sine.
Osc 2's wave in the Analog engine: Saw, Square, Triangle or Sine.
Osc 2's tuning against Osc 1 in semitones (-24 to +24), for octaves and fifths; in both engines.
Osc 2's fine tuning in cents (-50 to +50) for the classic beating of two detuned oscillators.
The balance between Osc 1 (0%) and Osc 2 (100%).
A sine one octave below Osc 1 (0 to 100%) for weight in basses and leads.
White noise added to every voice (0 to 100%), for breath and attack.
The wavetable for the Wavetable engine: Basic (sine to square), Pulse (width), Organ (drawbars), Vocal (vowels), Glass (high partials), Sync, Fold and Digital; all made by synthesis, no files.
Where in the table it reads (0 to 100%): the table's frames morph smoothly into each other.
The filter: Low Pass, Band Pass or High Pass.
The filter's steepness: 12 dB or 24 dB per octave.
The filter's cutoff frequency (20 Hz to 20 kHz).
The resonance (0 to 100%): a peak at the cutoff, close to whistling at the top.
How far the filter envelope moves the cutoff (-100 to +100%, up to six octaves either way).
How much the cutoff follows the key (0 to 100%; 100% keeps the same brightness on every note).
The filter envelope's attack time (1 ms to 10 s).
The filter envelope's decay time (1 ms to 10 s).
The filter envelope's sustain level (0 to 100%).
The filter envelope's release time after the key is let go (1 ms to 10 s).
The amp envelope's attack time (1 ms to 10 s): short for plucks, long for pads.
The amp envelope's decay time (1 ms to 10 s).
The amp envelope's sustain level (0 to 100%); at 0 every note dies away like a pluck.
The amp envelope's release time after the key is let go (1 ms to 10 s).
The LFO's shape: Sine, Triangle, Square, Saw or Random (a new value each cycle).
The LFO's rate in Hz (0.05 to 20) when LFO Sync is Off.
Locks the LFO to a note value of the host tempo (1/1 to 1/16, triplets and dotted), in step with the beat while the host plays.
How far the LFO bends the pitch (0 to 12 semitones); the mod wheel adds a vibrato of up to half a semitone.
How far the LFO moves the cutoff (0 to 4 octaves), for wobbles and sweeps.
How far the LFO moves the wavetable Position (0 to 100%).
Glide time (0 to 2000 ms): notes slide from the previous pitch.
Poly plays up to 8 notes; Mono plays one and retriggers; Legato plays one and only glides between connected notes.
Oscillators per voice (1 to 4), detuned and spread across the stereo field for a thicker sound.
How far the Unison voices are detuned and panned (0 to 100%).
One macro for character (0 to 100%): drive before the filter, an octave of brightness and wider detune.
The built-in chorus's mix (0 to 100%), for width and movement.
The tempo-synced ping-pong delay's mix (0 to 100%).
The delay time as a note value at the host tempo (1/16 to 1/2, triplets and dotted).
How much of the delay comes back (0 to 90%); the repeats get darker.
The built-in reverb's mix (0 to 100%).
The reverb's size (0 to 100%): from a short room to a long, dark hall.
How much the velocity changes the loudness and the filter envelope (0 to 100%).
The pitch bend range in semitones (0 to 24).
Moves the whole instrument by octaves (-3 to +3).
The output level (-24 to +12 dB).

MPE: On for an MPE controller (lower zone): channel 1 stays the master channel, and on channels 2-16 each note gets its own pitch bend, pressure (louder, up to +6 dB) and CC74 timbre (the cutoff, ±2 octaves); Off treats every channel alike.
MPE Bend Range: how far a note's own pitch bend goes (48 semitones is the MPE default).
uses: Warm pads and evolving wavetable pads with chorus and a long reverb
Mono leads with glide, unison and a synced delay
Plucks, soft keys and arpeggios
Vintage string machine with four-voice unison and deep chorus
Analog, sub and wobble basses (LFO synced to the tempo)
Digital bells and organ tones from the built-in tables
synth.properties: An instrument: MIDI in, stereo out, no samples, 8 voices (a new note takes a silent voice, then the oldest released one, then the oldest; a sounding voice keeps its envelope and phases, so nothing clicks). Analog: PolyBLEP saw and square, triangle, sine. Wavetable: eight tables of eight frames made at load by synthesis (additive or one cycle through the FFT), band-limited per octave and read with linear interpolation between samples and frames. Per voice: a state-variable filter (12 or 24 dB, low, band or high pass), linear-attack exponential ADSRs for amp and filter. A global LFO (smoothed over 2 ms), sample-accurate MIDI with sustain pedal, mod wheel vibrato, pitch bend and all notes off, then chorus, ping-pong delay and an eight-line feedback delay network reverb. Deterministic (Park-Miller noise) and the same in the JSFX, the GFX version and the VST3/CLAP.

Runs the saturation at 2x or 4x the sample rate (linear-phase halfband filters, 31 or 37 more samples of latency) so its harmonics do not fold back as aliasing; Off adds nothing.

tape.properties: Signal chain: Input → Wow/Flutter Modulated Delay (3 ms centre, cubic interpolation) → Pre-Emphasis → Drive → Asymmetric Saturation with memory (hysteresis-like) → De-Emphasis → Low Cut + Head Bump → Hiss → High-Frequency Loss → Mix → Output. The hiss is an exact Park-Miller generator. The dry signal is delayed by the same 3 ms, and the 3 ms latency is reported to the host for delay compensation. Oversampling (2x / 4x) runs the saturation stage at the higher rate and adds 31 / 37 samples.

tape_echo.keywords: tape echo space echo multi-head delay repeat dub reggae spring reverb wow flutter saturation self-oscillation runaway vintage analog tempo sync freeze
slider_desc: Time between the record head and playback head 1 (50 to 1000 ms); heads 2 and 3 sit at twice and three times this distance. A change glides like a tape motor, so the echoes bend in pitch.
Locks head 1 to a note at the project tempo (straight, dotted or triplet); heads 2 and 3 follow at 2x and 3x. Off uses Repeat Time.
The classic 12-position selector: which playback heads you hear and feed back (1, 2, 3 and their combinations), the R positions add the spring reverb, and R alone is the reverb without echoes.
Feedback of the active heads into one shared loop; 100% is unity loop gain in every mode, above it the echo runs away into self-oscillation that the tape saturation keeps bounded.
Low shelf at 250 Hz on the echoes (-12 to +12 dB).
High shelf at 2.5 kHz on the echoes (-12 to +12 dB).
Tape wow (two slow sines, up to 2.5 ms) and flutter (two fast sines, up to 0.15 ms) moving every head together, so the repeats waver in pitch.
Tape drive inside the feedback loop: 0% only rounds very loud repeats, higher values squash and colour every repeat with asymmetric (even) harmonics.
Level of the spring reverb, heard in the R positions of the Heads selector; it is fed with the input and the echoes.
Blend between the dry signal and the echoes (plus the spring).
Stops recording and loops what is on the tape (the length of the longest active head) forever, without fading or building up.
uses: Dub and reggae echoes that build and run away under your hand
Rhythmic multi-head patterns from one repeat time
Slapback with tape colour on vocals and guitars
Spring-drenched surf and ambient washes in the R modes
Warbly lo-fi delays with heavy wow, flutter and saturation
tape_echo.properties: Signal chain: Input + loop → stereo tape (record head) → playback heads at 1x, 2x, 3x the repeat time (4-point Hermite reads, wow/flutter on all heads, the time glides over ~0.12 s) → heads of the selected mode summed → feedback loop: ÷ number of heads → 12 dB/oct low-pass at 4.5 kHz → asymmetric soft saturation (slope 1 at 0, bounded) → 90 Hz one-pole low cut → × Intensity back onto the tape. Echo output: heads ÷ √(number of heads) → Bass (low shelf 250 Hz) → Treble (high shelf 2.5 kHz) → + spring tank in the R modes (two dispersive 40-stage all-pass springs, 2.2 s decay, fed with input and echoes) → Dry/Wet Mix. Tape length 6.75 s (3 × a dotted quarter at 40 bpm); zero latency.

PPM: a peak follower charging with a 5 ms time constant (about -4 dB on a 10 ms burst) and falling 24 dB in 2.8 s, -24 to +12 around the reference. K-14 / K-20: RMS over 300 ms, sine-calibrated. OVER lights for 1 s at 0 dBFS. The audio passes through (Monitor folds it after the meters). No latency, no Rack module.

slider_desc: Pedal position from heel (0%) to toe (100%) in Manual mode, smoothed over 15 ms; automate it or map a MIDI CC to it.
Manual: the Pedal slider moves the filter. Auto: an envelope follower moves it with your playing dynamics. LFO: a smooth sweep at Rate or in time with the project.
Classic: the inductor wah's narrow peak from about 400 Hz to 2.2 kHz. Vocal: two formant peaks that move together like a vowel changing. Wide: a broader sweep from 200 Hz to 3.5 kHz.
Sharpness of the peak: more Resonance gives a narrower, more vocal quack.
Auto mode: how loud you must play to reach the toe, from 0 dBFS at 0% down to -42 dBFS at 100% (the pedal moves over the 30 dB below that).
Auto mode: how fast the envelope follower opens the filter (1 to 100 ms).
Auto mode: how fast the filter falls back after a note (20 to 1000 ms).
LFO mode: sweeps per second when Tempo Sync is off (0.1 to 10 Hz).
LFO mode: one full sweep per note at the project tempo (1/1 to 1/16), locked to the bar while the transport plays.
Blend between the dry signal and the wah.
Level after the wah (-12 to +12 dB); the wah is already level-matched to its input, so 0 dB sits at the bypassed level.
uses: Classic wah on guitar, automated or played from a MIDI expression pedal
Funky auto-wah (envelope filter) on clean guitar, bass and clavinet

wah.properties: Signal chain: pedal position (Manual: smoothed slider; Auto: peak envelope follower with Attack/Release mapped over 30 dB below the Sensitivity level; LFO: raised cosine at Rate or one cycle per note, beat-locked while playing) → exponential frequency curve per model → TPT state-variable band-pass (Q 2-10 Classic, 3-10 Vocal with a second formant at 0.7 level, 1.2-6.2 Wide), normalised to 0 dB peak and lifted by +3.5 to +9.5 dB with Resonance → level match to the input (powers smoothed over 1 s, gain -12 to +24 dB) → Dry/Wet Mix → Output. The filter is modulated every sample; zero latency.
